section_summary: This section assesses Japan’s foreign exchange reserves and its ability to finance continued war in China, comparing Treasury and State Department estimates of gold, bank balances, and securities. Later documents show how Japanese exchange controls affected American firms seeking payment or remittance, especially cotton traders. The section also examines whether cotton import permits discriminated against American cotton and ends with an inquiry about a blocked publishing account.

people.role: Chief, Finance Division, Department of Commerce

people.name: C. F. Remer
people.role: Author of Foreign Investments in China

people.name: E. F. Creekmore
people.role: Vice President and General Manager, American Cotton Cooperative Association

subfiles.title: Analysis of Japan’s foreign exchange resources and wartime payments
subfiles.about: Estimates Japan’s available foreign exchange and the rate at which war and trade deficits would consume it.
subfiles.summary: The analysis puts Japan’s potentially available foreign exchange resources at about $475 million and estimates a possible 1938 drain of roughly $55 million monthly if hostilities continue. It reviews trade, invisible payments, capital movements, gold recovery, securities sales, and possible emergency measures. A war involving the Soviet Union would greatly worsen Japan’s position, particularly without foreign credit.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Treasury memorandum on Japan’s reserves
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Treasury studies on Japan’s reserves and current trade.
subfiles.summary: Hull says the State Department is revising its own study and will send Treasury copies.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on Patton’s estimates
subfiles.about: Comments on the agreement among three estimates of Japanese foreign exchange resources.
subfiles.summary: Patton’s check differs little from Treasury’s estimate; all three studies are considered mutually supportive.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of comments on Treasury’s memorandum
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Forwards technical comments and a comparison of estimates.
subfiles.summary: The adviser forwards comments and promises a further summary of Japan’s exchange position.

subfiles.title: Comments on Treasury Department’s confidential memorandum on Japan’s foreign exchange resources
subfiles.from: H. S. Patton, Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Checks Treasury’s estimate of Japanese gold, foreign balances, securities, and external obligations.
subfiles.summary: Patton estimates Japan’s total gold holdings near $300 million in mid-December but finds less gold freely usable under existing currency law than Treasury assumed. He examines newly mined gold, dollar balances, the uncertain marketability of Japanese-owned foreign securities, and the likely declining value of Japanese external bonds. His total estimate of realizable resources, $470 million, nearly matches Treasury’s $475 million, while his estimate of immediately usable first-line resources is lower.

subfiles.title: Draft acknowledgment of Treasury memorandum
subfiles.about: Drafts the acknowledgment appearing in final form on page 90.
subfiles.summary: Thanks Treasury for its reserve memorandum and trade report; promises a revised State Department study.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of State Department comments to Treasury
subfiles.about: Sends technical comments on Treasury’s Japan reserves memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses State Department comments and a comparison with its earlier estimate.

subfiles.title: Request for Tokyo’s information on Japanese foreign securities
subfiles.about: Requests estimates of Japanese-held foreign securities’ realizable dollar value.
subfiles.summary: Asks Tokyo to assess foreign securities, excluding Chinese and Manchukuoan obligations, and their conversion basis.

subfiles.title: Japanese-owned foreign currency securities
subfiles.about: Requests detailed information on Japanese-owned foreign assets and exchange conversion methods.
subfiles.summary: Jones asks why new legal authority was needed to compel liquidation of foreign assets and seeks updated holdings, conversion rates, and evidence of liquidity. He questions published claims about Japanese holdings of American and European bonds and supplies Treasury statistics that cannot isolate Japan from other Far Eastern countries.

subfiles.title: Tokyo reply on foreign securities information
subfiles.about: Reports that available securities information was sent by the commercial attaché.
subfiles.summary: Refers the Department to the commercial attaché’s December 23 letter to the Finance Division.

subfiles.title: Department of State charge slip
subfiles.about: Records a file charge.
subfiles.summary: Administrative charge slip with a 1949 notation.

subfiles.title: Japanese bank balances in New York
subfiles.about: Records Treasury figures for Japanese bank balances in New York.
subfiles.summary: Treasury reports $45.2 million on December 8, against $45 million on November 24.

subfiles.title: Japanese bank balances in New York
subfiles.about: Duplicates the conversation memorandum on Japanese balances.
subfiles.summary: Repeats Treasury’s December 8 balance of $45.2 million.

subfiles.title: Secretary of the Treasury letterhead
subfiles.about: Letterhead page without readable correspondence.
subfiles.summary: Only Treasury letterhead and filing marks are visible.

subfiles.title: Purchase of Japanese national bonds by Ford Motor Company of Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Explains a bond purchase tied to permission to remit Ford’s dividends.
subfiles.summary: Ford’s representative says the Exchange Control Commission offered dividend remittance permits if the company bought one million yen in Japanese national bonds, which it did. Grew also reports that Singer Sewing Machine had been offered a similar arrangement but had not bought bonds and still held substantial blocked yen.

subfiles.title: Release of Orvis Brothers funds
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese Foreign Office response on funds owed to Orvis Brothers.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office reports release of 281,000 yen to Orvis Brothers’ Japanese clients; the Embassy seeks clarification of the full amount due.

subfiles.title: Introduction of cotton exporter E. Harold Saer
subfiles.about: Introduces Saer to explain a cotton payment problem involving Japan.
subfiles.summary: Creekmore asks Moore to meet Saer about unpaid 1937 cotton sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Creekmore on cotton exchange permits
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the association’s request for help obtaining dollar reimbursement.
subfiles.summary: The Department says it will ask its Tokyo embassy to raise Japan’s refusal to permit transfer of cotton margin payments.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Grew on American Cotton Cooperative Association claim
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to raise blocked cotton margin payments with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The association sold 13,450 bales for about $1.07 million, but exchange permits covered only the lower current market value, leaving a claimed difference of $325,226. The Department asks Grew to explain the resulting harm to the association and its Japanese business relationships.

subfiles.title: Conversation with E. Harold Saer on cotton payments
subfiles.about: Records Saer’s account of blocked payments for American cotton.
subfiles.summary: Saer explains that Japan will permit remittance at the current cotton price but not the higher contracted price. He asks for assistance and says American cotton shippers will not extend credit or ship on an open payment basis.

subfiles.title: Statement on American cotton contracts in default
subfiles.about: Sets out the association’s claim for cotton contract price differences.
subfiles.summary: Exchange restrictions block margin transfers on 13,450 bales, leaving a stated $325,226 difference.

subfiles.title: Creekmore thanks Moore
subfiles.about: Thanks Moore for assistance with the association’s cotton payment problem.
subfiles.summary: Creekmore requests updates and promises to report changes.

subfiles.title: Orvis requests a meeting
subfiles.about: Seeks a meeting about complications in transferring funds from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Orvis proposes visiting Washington on March 14.

subfiles.title: Hamilton’s reply to Orvis
subfiles.about: Responds to Orvis’s proposed March 14 visit.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says division officers will be available to discuss Orvis’s blocked funds.

subfiles.title: File note on exchange manipulation in North China
subfiles.about: Cross-references a memorandum on Japanese exchange measures in occupied areas.
subfiles.summary: Notes possible customs takeover and a new Peiping currency pegged to the yen.

subfiles.title: Orvis explains partial release and remaining blocked yen
subfiles.about: Explains how earlier permits worked and requests help releasing more yen.
subfiles.summary: Orvis says a silk export permit and a separate cotton goods shipment offered indirect means of recovering part of the funds, with costs and uncertainty. Approximately 400,000 additional yen remain blocked, while his firm must supply dollars against Japanese clients’ cotton margin obligations.

subfiles.title: Department reply on Orvis’s remaining funds
subfiles.about: Reports that the Embassy has been asked to raise Orvis’s remaining blocked funds.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says Tokyo will emphasize both the delayed permits for approximately 400,000 yen and the firm’s dollar obligations.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Grew on Orvis Brothers’ blocked funds
subfiles.from: Francis B. Sayre, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Asks the Embassy to pursue permits for Orvis Brothers’ remaining yen.
subfiles.summary: The Department corrects the impression that previously reported permits produced a direct dollar transfer: they enabled export transactions instead. It quotes Orvis’s account and asks the Embassy to stress the hardship from approximately 400,000 yen still blocked against dollar margin liabilities.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Orvis on blocked funds
subfiles.about: Records Orvis’s request to raise a larger blocked balance with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Jones asks Orvis to submit the full figures in writing for Department consideration.

subfiles.title: Orvis thanks the Department
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Department’s March 26 response.
subfiles.summary: Orvis thanks the Department for its help with blocked yen and cotton clearing obligations.

subfiles.title: File note on Osaka cotton despatch
subfiles.about: Calls attention to the December 11 Osaka despatch.
subfiles.summary: Says the despatch’s first page adequately summarizes its findings.

subfiles.title: Osaka report on Japanese cotton import permits
subfiles.from: Kenneth C. Krentz, American Consul, Osaka
subfiles.about: Investigates whether Japan’s cotton import permits discriminate against American cotton.
subfiles.summary: Krentz finds no evidence that permits favor Indian or other cotton origins; differing import patterns reflect earlier orders, shipping delays, seasons, and exchange restrictions. Limited funds may temporarily favor cheaper Indian cotton, and North China cotton could gain an advantage if available without foreign exchange, though supplies appear constrained.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about payment by Maruzen Company
subfiles.from: Henry A. Barton, American Institute of Physics
subfiles.about: Asks whether exchange controls explain delayed payment for American books and magazines.
subfiles.summary: Barton seeks official confirmation of restrictions affecting an approximately £4,500 account owed by Maruzen.
